newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes mixed in U.S. after sterling soars.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes mixed in U.S. after sterling soars.

text.p: The dollar closed mixed after earlier tumbling to a 19-month low against the British pound which surged in response to an unexpected increase in U.K. interest rates, dealers said.

Sterling/mark also advanced to 2.4680, its highest level since December 1994 after the Bank of England raised official interest rates 25 basis points to 6.0 percent -- the first increase since February 1995.
Undermined by its slide versus the pound, the dollar retreated further from Tuesday's 42-month high near 115 yen.

"Certainly dollar/sterling was a large part of it," said John McCarthy of ING Barings Capital Markets. "As we approached 115 yen and didn't break it, then fought our way back up to around 114.50 (on Wednesday), I think a round of profit-taking set in."
Sterling extended its recent rally to $1.6345 -- its highest level since March 1995. It ended at $1.6323/28, off slightly from $1.6330/35 at the open.
The dollar fell to 114.10/13 yen from 114.40/45.
But the U.S. currency managed to recoup early losses against the mark, closing at 1.5105/15 marks, up from 1.5082/87, as Germany's unit fell against the pound and yen.

After months of resisting the Bank of England's advice, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke surprised the markets by authorizing a rate hike so close to the general election which must be held by next May.
But Clarke's action enhanced the government's credibility and seemed to give investors a thumbs up to continue buying sterling for the benefit of its higher-yielding deposits.

"It was already up. Then of course the rate move was well accepted by the market and they pushed sterling even further, sterling/mark as well," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president at Credit Agricole in New York.
Conscious that higher interest rates could undermine the popularity of the already-embattled Conservative government, Clarke nonetheless said he was determined to nip possible inflation in the bud.
"The economy is performing exceptionally well," the Chancellor said.

"It's interesting because it sort of gives the impression they are content with the rise in sterling ... and perhaps we might even see higher levels from here," said Debra Doerr-Larsen, assistant vice president at Commerzbank.

Earlier, the mark got a short-lived boost against some European currencies amid ongoing questions about whether the European Union will block a French plan to transfer money from state-owned French Telecom to its national budget in order to meet fiscal conditions for entry to Europe's single currency.

Bundesbank council member Raimut Jochimsen criticized the French plan in a BBC television interview on Wednesday, saying it sent the wrong signal to other countries in the run-up to European Monetary Union.
The dollar ignored a government report showing U.S. gross domestic product rose just 2.2 percent in the third quarter, compared to 4.7 percent in the second quarter.

The dollar rose to 1.2545/55 Swiss francs from 1.2542/52 at the open and it fell to Canadian $1.3405/10 from C$1.3421/26. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7915/20 from $0.7929/34 at the open. -- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
